session.title: Who Does the Assembly Represent? — Objectives Resolution Resumes

primarySource.publisher: Parliament Digital Library, Lok Sabha Secretariat

transcriptReference.publisher: Constitution of India / Centre for Law and Policy Research
transcriptReference.note: Used for paragraph-level navigation and speaker segmentation; Parliament Digital Library remains canonical.

speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Opens Volume II by rebutting claims that the Assembly was merely a Hindu body, resolves a Cabinet Mission text discrepancy, organises the Steering Committee election and resumes the Objectives Resolution debate.

speakers.name: Satyanarayan Sinha
speakers.positionSummary: Moves the election of eleven members to the Steering Committee and explains its institutional functions.

speakers.name: Mohan Lal Saksena
speakers.positionSummary: Seconds the motion to elect the Steering Committee.

speakers.name: S. Radhakrishnan
speakers.positionSummary: Presents the Resolution as a necessary pledge for peaceful revolutionary transformation, popular sovereignty, rights, unity and a legally functioning constituent process.

speakers.name: N. V. Gadgil
speakers.positionSummary: Treats the Assembly as part of the freedom struggle, defends a single Union and links political liberty to economic justice and fundamental rights.

speakers.name: Vijayalakshmi Pandit
speakers.positionSummary: Places Indian independence within Asian and global anti-imperial freedom and argues that India must contribute to a freer world order.

speakers.name: N. G. Ranga
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that rights must be practically enforceable by workers, peasants and poor citizens, not merely declared on paper.

speakers.name: P. K. Sen
speakers.positionSummary: Describes the Resolution as a collective vow and asks members to remain conscious of the absent and unseen millions behind the visible Assembly.

speakers.name: S. Nagappa
speakers.positionSummary: Presses for real rather than merely textual equality of opportunity and political recognition for historically excluded communities.

speakers.name: Jagat Narain Lal
speakers.positionSummary: Treats the Resolution as a pledge backed by national determination and warns that the route to freedom depends partly on British conduct.

speakers.name: Algu Rai Shastri
speakers.positionSummary: Defends the Resolution through Indian historical and ethical traditions and rejects further obstruction or postponement.

interventions.summary: The President answers December statements in the British Parliament that depicted the Assembly as representing only Hindus. He places community attendance figures on record and distinguishes the Muslim League's absence from absence of all minorities.

Rajendra Prasad reports the inquiry into differing versions of paragraph 20 of the Cabinet Mission statement, explains how the Indian and parliamentary printings diverged and concludes that the difference does not materially alter the provision.

Satyanarayan Sinha moves election of eleven members to the Steering Committee and reads the rules defining its role in ordering business, grouping amendments and coordinating the Assembly's institutional work.
Mohan Lal Saksena seconds the Steering Committee motion.
The Chair puts the Steering Committee motion to the House, records its adoption, announces the nomination and possible election schedule, and then returns to the Objectives Resolution.

Radhakrishnan identifies three questions—whether a declaration is necessary, whether the time is right, and whether the objectives need amendment—and argues that a clear declaration is essential to reassure doubters and absent groups.

He defends the goal of an Independent Sovereign Republic and frames the Assembly's experiment as a peaceful route to a profound political and socio-economic transformation rather than a sectional government.

Radhakrishnan argues for unity without coercive constitutional manipulation, discusses the place of the princely States and grouping, and stresses that no durable constitution can simply be imposed against governed peoples' wishes.

He couples socio-economic reconstruction with protection of the human spirit from excessive state encroachment, then argues that the Assembly is legally functioning and that adequate minority safeguards should lead to implementation of its Constitution.

Gadgil rejects the idea that members are merely constitutional technicians. He describes the Assembly as a stage in the freedom struggle and says its objective must be clear to the people whose sacrifices made the process possible.

He supports an Indian Union that gives constituent units room to develop while providing collective security and economic strength, and interprets the Resolution's rights and justice commitments as requiring substantive economic change.

Gadgil presses for an honest transfer of power and concludes with a vision of a society in which character outranks wealth, equality replaces humiliation and constitutional freedom has social purpose.

Vijayalakshmi Pandit locates the Constituent Assembly within a longer demand for independence and within Asian struggles against imperialism. She argues that a free India has obligations beyond itself and can contribute to a more equal international order.
Ranga welcomes the Resolution for combining liberty with actual enjoyment of rights, but warns that formal civil liberties mean little if poverty leaves citizens unable to exercise them.

He calls for practical institutional help that lets poor citizens seek judicial protection of fundamental rights, describes the masses as the real minorities, and urges constitutional sanctions that make declared rights enforceable.

P. K. Sen supports the Resolution as a vow of dedication and reminds the House that even a fully constituted chamber would stand for hundreds of millions who are not physically present, including currently absent political groups.

Nagappa supports the Resolution but insists that equal opportunity cannot remain in a statute book; it must translate into real participation and administrative power for historically excluded people.

He describes Scheduled Castes as a political minority produced by exclusion from administration, rejects endless competitive weightage and demands fairness to all communities while preserving safeguards for backward and tribal groups.

Jagat Narain Lal connects the Resolution to the long Congress demand for complete independence and a constituent assembly, treating it as a solemn national resolve whose peaceful fulfilment depends on whether Britain accepts the constitutional path.
Algu Rai Shastri supports the Resolution by linking popular rule, protection and non-discrimination to ethical and historical traditions from different periods of Indian history.

Speaking in Hindi, Shastri says the Assembly addresses India's people and historical memory, argues that reconciliation already justified earlier delay, and rejects any policy of indefinite obstruction.
The President adjourns the Assembly until 11 a.m. on 21 January 1947.
